To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 63-µ emission from atomic oxygen has a downward flux at 30 km that is about 2.5 × 10−6 W m−2, and that the flux is independent of the zenith angle.
we have observed OI 63-μm emission in the lower stratosphere at a flux level 2–3 times higher than previously reported.

(1) the downward flux of 63-µ m emission from atomic oxygen is (2.4± 0.5 ) × 10− 5 W m− 2 sr− 1; (2) this value is independent of zenith angle; and (3) this value is larger than expected from previous rocket measurements or theory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the thermosphere and ionosphere of the Earth.
the study of the upper atmosphere, particularly the thermosphere, using the emission of the 63 µm line of atomic oxygen.
the measurement of atomic oxygen emission at 63 µm from the lower thermosphere.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 63-µ emission is not a major source of atmospheric cooling at thermospheric heights.
the OI 63-µM flux is not as important as previously believed.
the downward flux of OI emission is larger than expected, but not large enough to warrant a re-evaluation of the role of OI as a source of cooling in the thermosphere.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the downward flux of 63 µm OI emission at balloon altitudes is (1.9 ± 0.4) × 10-5 W m-2 sr-1, and the zenith angle dependence of this flux is consistent with the theoretical expectation for a source of emission that is distributed over a large altitude region.
the OI emission at the 63 µm line is a very good indicator of the temperature at the altitude of 100 km, which is a good indicator of the global temperature at the altitude.
the downward flux of the OI 63-µ m emission is larger than previously thought and is independent of zenith angle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the OI emission at the ground state is not a good indicator of atmospheric cooling.
the OI 63-µM emission from the ground electronic states is not optically thin, which is contrary to the current understanding of this emission.
OI emission from the thermosphere is a major source of cooling, even at the low thermospheric altitutde of 30 km, and the downward flux is not optically-thick.
